Sequential AIPE Check for a Correlation Coefficient

Source: R/seq_aipe_r.R
seq_aipe_r.Rd

Checks, with the paired data collected so far, whether enough pairs are in hand for a confidence interval for a population correlation that is no wider than a chosen width, without assuming bivariate normality and without a planning value for the correlation. The Pearson product moment correlation, Kendall's tau, and Spearman's rho are available. This is the sequential accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE) procedure of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2019).

Usage

seq_aipe_r(
  x,
  y,
  width,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  method = c("pearson", "kendall", "spearman")
)

Arguments

x, y

Numeric vectors: the two variables observed so far on the same units, paired by position. They must have the same length, with at least 4 pairs; missing or infinite values are an error.

width

The target full width of the confidence interval for the population correlation (\(\omega\) in the cited article): the upper limit minus the lower limit. A single positive number less than 2: a correlation lies between -1 and 1, so an interval 2 or more wide would say nothing, and such a target is an error.

conf_level

The confidence level of the interval, a single number strictly between 0 and 1. Default 0.95.

method

Which correlation coefficient to estimate: "pearson" (the default), "kendall", or "spearman".

Value

An object of class c("smsd_check", "data.frame") (see smsd_check_methods for its print(), summary(), and tidy() methods) with one row per quantity and columns term and value. The rows are, in order:

lower_limit

the lower confidence limit (NA when the variance estimate is not yet usable or the estimate cannot be computed; see the section below);

r

the estimated correlation (Pearson's r, Kendall's tau, or Spearman's rho, according to method, as cor computes it, so that with ties Kendall's tau is tau-b; NA when either variable has no variation);

upper_limit

the upper confidence limit (NA whenever lower_limit is);

xi_squared

the estimated asymptotic variance \(\hat{\xi}_n^2\), at least \(n^{-3}\) (the bound itself when the estimate is not yet usable);

criterion_n

the number of pairs the stopping rule currently requires (at least current_n + 1 when the variance estimate is not yet usable or the estimate cannot be computed);

current_n

the current number of pairs.

The object also carries these attributes:

is_satisfied

TRUE when the stopping rule is met, otherwise FALSE; never NA, and always identical to current_n >= criterion_n;

method

a string such as "Pearson correlation", with the name of the coefficient that method selects;

cor_method

the value of the argument method;

current_n, criterion_n

the values in the rows of those names;

conf_level, width

the values supplied;

variance_unusable

TRUE when the raw variance estimate is zero, negative, or not finite (see the section below), otherwise FALSE;

notes

a character vector, empty unless something needs explaining.

Details

The function evaluates the stopping rule once and returns. The user collects the pilot sample (see seq_aipe_r_pilot), calls seq_aipe_r(), and, while the rule is not met, adds one or more pairs and calls it again. The function prints nothing and keeps no state.

Stopping rule. Sampling stops at the first \(n\), at or after the pilot size, with $$n \ge \left\lceil \frac{4 z_{\alpha/2}^2}{\omega^2} \left(\hat{\xi}_n^2 + \frac{1}{n}\right) \right\rceil$$ (their Equation 10 for the Pearson correlation, Equation 30 for Kendall's tau, and Equation 54 for Spearman's rho), where \(\hat{\xi}_n^2\) estimates the asymptotic variance of \(\sqrt{n}\) times the sample correlation. The reported interval is \(r_n \pm z_{\alpha/2} \hat{\xi}_n / \sqrt{n}\) (their Equation 11). It is symmetric on the correlation scale: the article does not transform to Fisher's z, and neither does the package, so a limit can fall outside \([-1, 1]\) at small sample sizes. Whenever the rule is met, the width of the interval is at most width.

Variance estimators. For the Pearson correlation, \(\hat{\xi}_n^2\) is the moment based estimator of the article's Equation 70, a sample version of the distribution free variance in its Equation 3 (which equals \((1 - \rho^2)^2\) under bivariate normality). Equation 70 is printed with divisions by the sample covariance; the factor \(r_n^2\) in front cancels them, and the estimate is computed with that cancellation carried out, so that it is defined when the sample covariance is exactly zero (which happens with discrete data such as ratings). For Kendall's tau it is the estimator of the article's Equations 27 to 29. For Spearman's rho it is the estimator of Kojadinovic and Yan (2010) given as the article's Equations 51 to 53. (The article states its Spearman stopping rule with the estimator of Genest and Favre, 2007, its Equation 45, and offers Equation 51 as a simpler consistent alternative; Equation 51 is what the package computes, and it reproduces the article's Table 10.)

Tied values. The Kendall and Spearman variance estimators assume continuous data. With tied values (ratings on a 5 point scale, for example) they are too small, so the rule stops too early and the interval is too narrow: with bivariate normal data (\(\rho = 0.5\)) cut into five categories, the estimates averaged 78% (Kendall) and 85% (Spearman) of the actual sampling variance at \(n = 200\), and 95% intervals at that fixed sample size covered 91% and 92% of the time (6,000 simulated samples). The function warns, once per call, when method is "kendall" or "spearman" and either variable has tied values. With ties the Kendall estimate reported is also a different coefficient from the one the variance estimator belongs to: it is tau-b, as cor computes it, whereas the article's estimator (its Equation 23) is the average over pairs of observations of the product of the signs of their differences (tau-a). The two are the same number when there are no ties and can differ materially when there are: 0.334 against 0.265 for 200 bivariate normal pairs with \(\rho = 0.5\), both variables cut into five categories.

A perfect sample correlation. A sample correlation of 1 or \(-1\) (to within rounding error) says nothing about its own sampling variance. For the Pearson correlation the variance estimate is then zero, and so is the Kendall estimate for pairs ordered in opposite ways on the two variables; the Kendall estimate for pairs ordered the same way, and the Spearman estimate for pairs ordered either way, are positive, and with them the rule as printed would be met at once with a limit outside \([-1, 1]\) (\(-1.04\) and \(-0.96\) for Spearman's rho with 12 pairs in exactly reversed order at width = 0.4). The function treats the three alike: the variance estimate of a perfect sample correlation is not yet usable (see the section below), so the rule is reported as not met until a pair breaks the perfect order.

What the guarantee is. The width guarantee is exact. The coverage guarantee is asymptotic: coverage approaches conf_level as width shrinks (their Theorem 1). At wide targets, and so small final sample sizes, coverage falls short, and the article says so: its Table 2 reports coverage of 0.90 for a 95% interval of width 0.2 when \(\rho = 0.5\), and its Appendix D attributes the shortfall to the bias of the ratios of moment estimates in the variance estimator at small \(n\), which makes the procedure stop early. In simulated studies for this package (bivariate normal data, a 95% Pearson interval, the default m_0, one pair added at each stage), coverage was 0.93 for \(\rho = 0.4\) and 0.69 for \(\rho = 0.8\) at width = 0.2 (5,000 and 10,000 studies), and 0.78 and 0.69 at width = 0.4 (10,000 studies each). A large correlation is the hard case: its interval is short, so the rule can be met with few pairs (about 43 on average for \(\rho = 0.8\) at width = 0.2), and in samples that small the variance estimate is often unusable (it was zero or negative in 42% of the pilot samples in that condition, and in 14% for \(\rho = 0.4\) at width = 0.4) and otherwise tends to run low. When it is positive but below \(n^{-3}\) the bound is used, as the article prescribes, and the rule is then met with an interval far narrower than requested: in other runs of 6,000 studies at width = 0.4, 58 with \(\rho = 0.8\) and 10 with \(\rho = 0.4\) ended that way, and in runs of 2,000 at width = 0.2, 10 and none. A larger minimum pilot helps: with m_0 = 50 the coverages were 0.93 and 0.83 at width = 0.2 and 0.92 and 0.83 at width = 0.4. For Kendall's tau and Spearman's rho with \(\rho = 0.4\), coverage was 0.94 and 0.94 at width = 0.2 and 0.91 and 0.87 at width = 0.4; their variance estimates were never zero or below the lower bound. A stronger association is the hard case for them too: with \(\rho = 0.8\) or \(-0.8\), coverage was 0.91 to 0.92 for Kendall's tau and 0.87 to 0.88 for Spearman's rho at width = 0.2, and 0.89 to 0.91 and 0.84 to 0.85 at width = 0.4 (0.91 and 0.85 for \(\rho = 0.8\) in 10,000 studies). For a negative association the Kendall interval covers a little less often at a wide target than for a positive one of the same size: at width = 0.4 coverage was 0.90 for \(\rho = -0.4\), and 0.89 for \(\rho = -0.95\) against 0.93 for \(\rho = 0.95\) (6,000 studies each); at width = 0.2 it was 0.94 for \(\rho = -0.4\) and for \(\rho = -0.95\) (2,000 studies each). A strongly negative association can also make a small sample perfectly discordant (any two pairs ordered in opposite ways on the two variables). Kendall's tau is then \(-1\) and its variance estimate is zero, so the check is not yet usable until a concordant pair has been observed; this happened in 91 of the 6,000 pilot samples of 10 pairs with \(\rho = -0.95\), in 5 with \(\rho = -0.8\), and in none of the pilot samples of 20 pairs. Use seq_aipe_r_sensitivity to study a planned Pearson correlation study before collecting data, and prefer a narrow target or a larger m_0 when the correlation may be large.

Estimates That Are Not Yet Usable

When the raw variance estimate is zero (exactly, or to within rounding error), negative, or not finite, which is common at small sample sizes for some effect sizes, or when the point estimate cannot be computed (a sample with no variation, where values that agree to ten significant digits count as equal), the check reports the stopping rule as not met, sets attr(out, "variance_unusable") to TRUE, and attaches a note that print() shows; see smsd_check_methods. This is a deliberate departure from the stopping rule as printed in the source articles, under which the lower bound \(n^{-3}\) would stand in for such an estimate and the rule would be met at once with an interval far narrower than requested; a positive estimate, however small, is used as the articles prescribe (the larger of it and \(n^{-3}\)).

References

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2019). Sequential accuracy in parameter estimation for population correlation coefficients. Psychological Methods, 24(4), 492–515. doi:10.1037/met0000203

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243. doi:10.1037/met0000127

Genest, C., & Favre, A.-C. (2007). Everything you always wanted to know about copula modeling but were afraid to ask. Journal of Hydrologic Engineering, 12, 347–368. doi:10.1061/(ASCE)1084-0699(2007)12:4(347)

Kojadinovic, I., & Yan, J. (2010). Comparison of three semiparametric methods for estimating dependence parameters in copula models. Insurance: Mathematics and Economics, 47, 52–63. doi:10.1016/j.insmatheco.2010.03.008

Maxwell, S. E., Kelley, K., & Rausch, J. R. (2008). Sample size planning for statistical power and accuracy in parameter estimation. Annual Review of Psychology, 59, 537–563. doi:10.1146/annurev.psych.59.103006.093735

See also

seq_aipe_r_pilot for the pilot size and seq_aipe_r_sensitivity to simulate the Pearson procedure before collecting data. In DMAR: ss_aipe_r, the fixed sample size analog for when a planning value of the correlation is available, and ci_r, a fixed sample size confidence interval.

Other seq_aipe_r: seq_aipe_r_pilot(), seq_aipe_sensitivity

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Francis Bilson Darku fbilsond@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# How strongly are citizenship behavior at work and neuroticism related?
# The aim is a 95% confidence interval for the correlation that is no
# wider than 0.30.
set.seed(113)
new_pairs <- function(k, rho = -0.3) {
  citizenship <- rnorm(k)
  cbind(citizenship, rho * citizenship + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(k))
}
scores <- new_pairs(seq_aipe_r_pilot(width = 0.30))
out <- seq_aipe_r(scores[, 1], scores[, 2], width = 0.30)
out
#> Sequential check (Pearson correlation)
#> 
#>   Current n       : 14
#>   Criterion n     : 102
#>   Target width    : 0.3
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : -0.7589524
#>   r                 : -0.3790672
#>   upper_limit       : 0.0008179968
#>   xi_squared        : 0.5259405
#>   criterion_n       : 102
#>   current_n         : 14
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

# The rule is not met at the pilot. Add one employee at a time and check
# again, until it is.
while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {
  scores <- rbind(scores, new_pairs(1))
  out <- seq_aipe_r(scores[, 1], scores[, 2], width = 0.30)
}
out
#> Sequential check (Pearson correlation)
#> 
#>   Current n       : 125
#>   Criterion n     : 124
#>   Target width    : 0.3
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : -0.3967731
#>   r                 : -0.2487647
#>   upper_limit       : -0.1007562
#>   xi_squared        : 0.7128316
#>   criterion_n       : 124
#>   current_n         : 125
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE

# Kendall's tau from the same data and target
seq_aipe_r(scores[, 1], scores[, 2], width = 0.30, method = "kendall")
#> Sequential check (Kendall correlation)
#> 
#>   Current n       : 125
#>   Criterion n     : 70
#>   Target width    : 0.3
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : -0.2759581
#>   r                 : -0.1654194
#>   upper_limit       : -0.05488058
#>   xi_squared        : 0.397597
#>   criterion_n       : 70
#>   current_n         : 125
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE
